whyThisMatters: Real payment decisions are fast — an invoice lands, a deadline looms, and you don't always get time to research whether a request is safe. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a matching PO number, a reply that confirms an address is active, a confident senior name. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why "Checked PO Reference Number" still only counts as a partial check, even though it's a real and useful habit.
Ask why replying to an email to confirm a bank change feels like verification but isn't.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like a check — like a matching PO number, a reply confirming receipt, or a number printed in the email itself — without realising none of these actually verify who is asking. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.text: Call back to confirm bank changes
bubbles.why: A call to a known number exposes fake bank-change requests before money moves.
Look-alike domains are how fraudsters pose as real suppliers and colleagues.
Reporting lets security block the scam before a colleague pays it.
Approved portals have controls that stop payments going to fraudsters.

bubbles.text: Check bank details in the vendor file
bubbles.why: Comparing against the vendor file catches swapped bank account numbers.

bubbles.text: Hold a payment until it is verified
bubbles.why: A short delay costs little; a sent fraudulent payment is rarely recovered.

bubbles.text: Match each invoice to a PO
bubbles.why: Invoices with no matching order are a common sign of invoice fraud.
Different bank details from the usual ones often mean a supplier was impersonated.
Checking the ledger stops fake overpayment claims from getting a refund.
A second pair of eyes often spots a scam you were pressured not to question.

bubbles.text: Change bank details on an email alone
bubbles.why: Emails are easily faked, so fraudsters use them to redirect payments to themselves.
Scammers invent urgency so you bypass the checks that would stop them.
Fake invoice files can install malware that steals passwords or locks your files.

bubbles.text: Wire money to a new account at once
bubbles.why: Money sent to a fraudster's new account is usually gone within hours.
A domain that doesn't match is a classic sign the sender is an impostor.
Fake overpayments trick staff into sending real money back to criminals.
Email can be intercepted, giving criminals what they need to commit fraud.

bubbles.text: Pay an invoice with no PO match
bubbles.why: Paying without a matching order lets fake invoices slip through.

bubbles.text: Obey an urgent request from a boss
bubbles.why: Criminals pose as executives and rush staff into paying before they think.
One person acting alone is easy to fool; two approvers catch more fraud.
Two approvers make it much harder for one tricked person to send fraud money.
A wrong or missing PO number is a quick way to spot a fake invoice.

bubbles.text: Call the number given in the email
bubbles.why: The number in a scam email connects you to the scammer, not the real company.

bubbles.text: Reply to the email to confirm changes
bubbles.why: Replying only reaches the sender, who may be the fraudster who made the request.
